section_1.title: Introduction: The Flatlander Paradox
section_1.content: Establish prerequisite knowledge by defining a 'dimension' as a degree of freedom. Introduce the concept of a 2D entity (Flatlander) unable to perceive depth, to help students conceptualize how we (3D beings) might look to a 4D entity.
section_1.example: An animation showing a square moving through a 2D line, vs. a sphere passing through a 2D plane appearing as a circle that grows and shrinks.

section_2.title: Mapping Dimensions: 1D to 2D to 3D
section_2.content: Teach the 'sweep' method: Drag a point to create a line (1D), drag a line to create a square (2D), drag a square to create a cube (3D). Define vertices and edges as the building blocks for extrapolation.
section_2.example: Visual transition: A dot (0D) → A segment (1D) → A square (2D) → A cube (3D), highlighting how each step introduces one new axis.

section_3.title: The Leap to 4D: The Tesseract
section_3.content: Apply the 'sweep' method to the 3D cube. By dragging a 3D cube along an invisible 'w' axis, we visualize the Tesseract (hypercube). Explain that while we can't 'see' 4D, we can project its 'shadow' into our 3D space.
section_3.example: An animation of a rotating Tesseract 'shadow'—a cube-within-a-cube where lines seem to pass through each other, demonstrating the spatial complexity of a 4D object.

section_4.title: Application: The Escape Puzzle
section_4.content: Challenge the students with a dimensional puzzle: How would a 2D creature escape a locked 2D square room? (By 'jumping' into the 3rd dimension). Analogize this to how a 4D entity could bypass any 3D physical barrier.
section_4.example: A cartoon '2D Cat' trapped in a drawn square on paper, suddenly vanishing by moving 'up' into the 3D space, demonstrating dimensional escape.

section_5.title: Conclusion: Summary and Perspective
section_5.content: Recap that dimensional shifting is about changing perspective. Emphasize that advanced geometry is essentially the study of how structures behave when we add a new spatial constraint.
section_5.example: A final visual of a 4D object collapsing back into a 3D cube, then a 2D square, reinforcing the concept of mathematical projection.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right
